prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: mild bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do not give ceftriaxone or cefotaxime: documented ceftriaxone hypersensitivity.
Do not attribute the fever, rash and somnolence to drug fever without a lumbar puncture: new somnolence, neck stiffness, photophobia and papilledema need CSF examination.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
required_recommendations: Give meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours with vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8 to 12 hours within 60 minutes, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture, withholding ceftriaxone for the documented maculopapular rash (meropenem also covers Listeria); the current meropenem 1 g every 8 hours is a prophylactic, sub-meningeal dose (IDSA 2017).

Adjunctive dexamethasone is not required here: WHO 2025 recommends starting it shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose, she has received parenteral meropenem and vancomycin for days before the meningitis was recognised, and no trial supports starting it after days of parenteral therapy; if it is given, stop it after a maximum of 4 days.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before escalating to meningeal-dose antibiotics.

Take blood cultures and give the first meningeal dose of antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of mild bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: S. pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin (MIC 0.06 mg/L) and meropenem; stop vancomycin and continue meropenem, or switch to benzylpenicillin after assessment of the cephalosporin allergy.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Involve neurosurgery to assess the anterior skull base repair for a persistent CSF leak, and repair the leak once the infection is controlled to prevent recurrence.
Offer pneumococcal conjugate vaccination after recovery: a CSF leak is an indication.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025).

Take blood cultures and give the first meningeal dose of antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of mild bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Adjunctive dexamethasone is started shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose (WHO 2025); a patient already on parenteral antibiotics for days is outside that evidence.

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.

A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia; a borderline ratio on antibiotics does not exclude bacterial meningitis.

Meningitis after neurosurgery, as here 10 days after dural repair, is treated with vancomycin plus meropenem or cefepime (IDSA 2017); with ceftriaxone hypersensitivity, meropenem 2 g every 8 hours is the beta-lactam.
Prophylactic antibiotic doses do not reach meningeal CSF concentrations; breakthrough meningitis on prophylaxis requires escalation to meningeal dosing.
Chronic CSF rhinorrhea after skull base fracture is a portal for pneumococcal meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: mild bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (recent neurosurgery). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and meningeal-dose antibiotics given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025).

metadata.adaptation_notes: Source case was a 14-year-old diagnosed with drug fever post-EBP. This case inverts the diagnostic conclusion: the same clinical setup (post-neurosurgical patient with dural repair, CSF drain, EBP, rash, and fever) is used, but the underlying diagnosis is true bacterial meningitis that initially masquerades as drug fever. Age adjusted to 22 to meet schema constraints (18-90). Clinical complexity and red herrings from the source case are preserved and amplified.
metadata.difficulty_description: Initial presentation strongly mimics drug fever with concurrent rash, eosinophilia, and temporal relationship to medications and EBP. CSF is ambiguous with mixed pleocytosis and borderline glucose. The key diagnostic evidence (elevated CSF lactate, worsening trajectory, positive cultures) requires follow-up investigations and careful clinical reasoning to distinguish from the more benign drug-fever interpretation.

patient.history_present_illness: A 22-year-old woman presents with fever, rash, and altered mental status in the neurosurgical step-down unit. She sustained frontal sinus fractures and a basilar skull fracture in a motor vehicle accident eight months ago, complicated by intermittent cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea. Ten days ago, she underwent surgical debridement and obliteration of the frontal sinuses with dural repair of an anterior cranial fossa defect. A lumbar CSF drain was placed intraoperatively and removed five days ago. During her perioperative course, she developed a pruritic maculopapular rash attributed to ceftriaxone, which resolved when antibiotics were changed to meropenem and vancomycin. After removal of the lumbar drain, she developed a severe positional headache with nausea, vomiting, and refusal to ambulate, consistent with post-dural puncture headache. Imaging at that time demonstrated a bifrontal extradural CSF collection. Three days ago, she received an epidural blood patch with 15 mL of autologous blood one interspace above the lumbar drain site, which significantly improved her orthostatic symptoms. Approximately 18 hours after the epidural blood patch, nursing noted that she was flushed and febrile to 38.8 degrees Celsius. She was no longer orthostatic and denied nausea or vomiting at that time. However, approximately 3 hours later she developed pruritus of the arms and legs with a fine maculopapular rash similar to her earlier ceftriaxone-related eruption. The primary team initially attributed the fever and rash to drug fever, potentially related to continued diphenhydramine or a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Over the subsequent 2 days, however, the patient has become increasingly somnolent with worsening headache that is no longer purely positional. She now reports photophobia and diffuse, constant headache rated 9 out of 10.
